definition: a count or total; to agree or correspond
memoryTip: Marks on a stick that add up — the counts match.
correctPassage: The final vote tally confirmed that the amendment had failed by a narrow margin.
wrongPassages: She tried to tally the rival firm by undercutting every bid without reading the specs.
The engineer described the circuit as tally once the breaker tripped under load.
He negotiated a tally settlement by refusing any written record of the terms.

memoryTip: Like a dusty nebula — cloudy, vague, not sharply defined.
correctPassage: Critics called the mission statement nebulous because it never defined success.
wrongPassages: The engineer’s nebulous blueprint specified every measurement to the millimeter.
After the numbered checklist, nobody found the steps nebulous—each had a diagram.
She labeled the crystal a nebulous solid after it held its shape under pressure.

memoryTip: Doesn’t assume airs — quiet and modest.
correctPassage: Despite her fame, she remained unassuming and preferred to work without publicity.
wrongPassages: The unassuming CEO demanded a motorcade and a private floor for every visit.
Reviewers called the speech unassuming after he named himself the sole author of the reform.
Her unassuming wardrobe featured only designer labels and a staff of stylists.

memoryTip: Out + size — bigger than the usual size.
correctPassage: The museum devoted an outsize share of its budget to a single traveling exhibit.
wrongPassages: They hoped to outsize the protest by moving public comment after midnight.
He moved to outsize the deposition by reading a prepared statement for every answer.
Analysts called the startup’s market share outsize after it sold fewer than twenty units.

memoryTip: In-extricable: can’t extract yourself — tangled tight.
correctPassage: In the novel, personal loyalty and political ambition become inextricable.
wrongPassages: The two cables were inextricable: one tug separated them cleanly in seconds.
She filed an inextricable appeal that the court dismissed for lack of any supporting brief.
His inextricable sketch caught the likeness in a few decisive lines and nothing more.

definition: not in harmony; out of place
memoryTip: In-congruent: doesn’t “fit” the picture; out of place.
correctPassage: A neon sign looked incongruous against the centuries-old stone facade.
wrongPassages: The navy suit was incongruous with the formal dress code and drew no second glances.
Editors praised the chapter as incongruous because every scene advanced the same theme.
Her incongruous color scheme matched the room’s palette down to the trim.

memoryTip: Im-pertinent: not “pertaining” politely — rude and out of line.
correctPassage: The reporter’s impertinent questions about private finances angered the candidate.
wrongPassages: The clerk’s impertinent reply restated the policy and offered three clear next steps.
Judges called the brief impertinent for citing every relevant statute with care.
Her impertinent silence during the award speech was taken as deep respect.

memoryTip: Can’t surmount (climb over) it — too big a barrier.
correctPassage: What had seemed an insurmountable funding gap was closed by a single anonymous gift.
wrongPassages: The trail was so insurmountable that first-time hikers finished early without maps.
They treated the checklist as insurmountable and cleared every item before lunch.
Once the password reset worked, the login barrier proved entirely insurmountable.

definition: the quality of being calm and peaceful
memoryTip: Tranquil + ity — calm lake, quiet mind.
correctPassage: After the storm, a rare sense of tranquility settled over the harbor.
wrongPassages: The market’s tranquility showed in triple-digit swings and halted trading.
Residents fled the tranquility of sirens and continuous construction noise.
He sought tranquility by scheduling three overlapping deadlines for the same afternoon.

definition: a temporary relief from something unpleasant
memoryTip: A brief relief before the hard thing resumes — temporary break.
correctPassage: A last-minute injunction granted the tenants a temporary reprieve from eviction.
wrongPassages: The clinic tried to reprieve no-shows by double-booking every appointment slot.
After the verdict, the sentence was a permanent reprieve with no chance of review.
She called the longer workday a welcome reprieve from free evenings at home.

definition: not allowing passage; unable to be affected
memoryTip: Im-pervious: nothing can pierce through (water, criticism).
correctPassage: The coating is nearly impervious to water and salt air.
wrongPassages: The sponge was impervious to the spill and soaked through within seconds.
He tried to impervious the callers by parking them on mute without answering.
Critics found her open to every critique, utterly impervious and quick to revise.

definition: not able to be defended or maintained
memoryTip: Can’t tenably hold it — the argument collapses; position is indefensible.
correctPassage: Once the data were corrected, the original hypothesis became untenable.
wrongPassages: The peer-reviewed model remained untenable under every independent replication.
She treated the requirement as untenable after the client waived it in writing.
Historians called the archive untenable because every claim matched primary sources.

memoryTip: Ubi = where (Latin) — seems to be everywhere you look.
correctPassage: Smartphones are now so ubiquitous that many public spaces assume constant connectivity.
wrongPassages: Rotary phones are ubiquitous here: one sits on every modern classroom desk.
The orchid is ubiquitous—only a single wild specimen has ever been found.
He kept his ubiquitous diary in one locked drawer no visitor ever saw.

memoryTip: De-funct: function stopped — dead, no longer running.
correctPassage: The defunct railway line has been converted into a walking path.
wrongPassages: The defunct clinic still books patients seven days a week and posts daily wait times.
Investors poured capital into the defunct startup after record quarterly growth.
She marked the live feed defunct while thousands watched the stream in real time.

definition: a person who criticizes or disparages someone or something
memoryTip: De-tract: pulls reputation down — a critic who knocks you.
correctPassage: Even the project’s fiercest detractor admitted the design was elegant.
wrongPassages: The lead sponsor acted as chief detractor, funding the tour and praising every stop.
She hired a detractor to write glowing blurbs for the dust jacket.
His lifelong detractor never missed a premiere and always led the standing ovation.

memoryTip: Exhausts every option — complete, thorough, nothing left out.
correctPassage: An exhaustive review of the literature found no support for the claim.
wrongPassages: The exhaustive summary skipped half the chapters and cited no sources.
Viewers found the two-minute recap exhaustive for crushing all shadow detail.
An exhaustive search of one drawer turned up the missing key on the first try.

memoryTip: Hetero = different — a mixed, diverse group.
correctPassage: The sample was deliberately heterogeneous, including rural and urban schools.
wrongPassages: The team was so heterogeneous that every member shared the same degree and hometown.
Lab notes described a heterogeneous alloy of one pure metal and nothing else.
Critics called the playlist heterogeneous after every track used the same tempo and key.

memoryTip: Like an imperative sentence (command) — must-do, essential.
correctPassage: With the storm approaching, it was imperative that residents evacuate promptly.
wrongPassages: The bureau hoped to imperative backlog age by resetting ticket clocks nightly.
Choosing a font color was imperative to the reactor’s safety review.
They postponed the imperative step because nothing of consequence depended on it.

definition: a subtle difference in meaning or expression
memoryTip: A fine shade of meaning — subtle, not black-and-white.
correctPassage: The translation preserved every nuance of the original poem’s tone.
wrongPassages: The billboard’s nuance was a single bold slogan visible from a mile away.
Her nuance bibliography cited only URLs that returned 404 errors.
He preferred blunt labels and said nuance was just another word for shouting.

memoryTip: Causes controversy — people argue about it.
correctPassage: The museum’s controversial exhibit drew both praise and protests.
wrongPassages: The controversial rule change passed unanimously and drew no public comment at all.
Boards postponed the controversial safety retrofit that every inspector and parent had already endorsed.
Analysts called the quiet consensus vote the most controversial outcome of an uneventful session.
